title: NAS 410 Audit Documentation for Hartford Suppliers
description: NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 audit documents for Hartford-area engine part, repair and special-process suppliers, ready for your Level 3. Contact Atlantis.
h1: NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 Audit Documentation for Hartford-Area Engine and Aerospace Suppliers
html:
Central Connecticut's aerospace economy runs on jet engines and the parts, coatings and repairs that keep them flying, and nearly every supplier in that chain with an NDT process is audited against NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114. Atlantis NDT supports Hartford-area engine part makers, repair suppliers and special process houses by preparing and reviewing their audit documentation, which the company's Responsible Level 3 then approves. Tell us about your next audit; we reply within one business day.

Our part, and the part that stays with your Responsible Level 3

Every NAS 410 program has an employer that certifies and a designated Level 3 who answers for the program technically. Neither of those roles transfers to Atlantis. Atlantis is not the Responsible Level 3 for your company or any other, does not issue NAS 410 certifications to anyone, and does not offer NAS 410 training or examinations. Your management designates the Responsible Level 3 in writing, that person approves the written practice, procedures, techniques and examinations, and your company certifies each technician under its own written practice.

What Atlantis brings is ASNT NDT Level III consulting aimed at the evidence an engine-sector auditor reviews. Leading it is Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT Level III whose five methods are UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, with eleven-plus years of NDT practice in several countries. Where your program's techniques fall in a method outside those certifications, a Level 3 who holds that method approves them, and our help stays on the record-keeping side. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States; on an RT program we limit ourselves to Level III review of procedures and records.

The engine corridor along the Connecticut River

Pratt & Whitney anchors the region, with its headquarters and engineering in East Hartford and engine production in Middletown, where a horizontal assembly line was built to support the PW1100G-JM geared turbofan for the Airbus A320neo family and the F135 engine for the F-35. North of the city, the Windsor Locks campus that once belonged to UTC Aerospace Systems remains a center for aircraft systems engineering under Collins Aerospace. Sikorsky's helicopter operations sit in Stratford, on the coast, and additive manufacturing has a foothold in South Windsor, where Oxford Performance Materials opened a facility for printed high-performance thermoplastic parts.

Around those names is a dense web of machine shops, blade and vane specialists, coating houses, heat treaters and NDT providers in towns such as Bloomfield, South Windsor, Manchester, Windsor and East Hartford. State leaders have said openly that the Connecticut supply chain had to nearly double its capacity to keep up with engine and airframe demand, and that smaller producers would feel the strain most. NDT programs are one of the places that strain shows: more parts, more customers and more audits, run by the same small quality teams.

The region's NDT work is shaped by the hardware. Rotating engine parts in nickel and titanium alloys, cases and structural castings, blades and vanes with coatings, steel gears and shafts, and the tooling and fixtures that support them all pass through penetrant, eddy current, ultrasonic and magnetic particle inspection somewhere between the mill and the engine.

From making engine parts to repairing them

A recent shift is changing what Hartford-area suppliers are audited on. Pratt & Whitney has brought third-party companies into its geared turbofan repair network for the first time, and the announced group included Connecticut firms Turbine Controls in Bloomfield, TWIN Manufacturing in South Windsor and AdChem Manufacturing Technologies in Manchester, alongside StandardAero and Lewis & Saunders. Several shops that grew up making new detail parts are now repairing used ones, and that changes the NDT program in ways that show up quickly at audit.

Inspecting a used part is not the same as inspecting a new one. Service-exposed hardware carries coatings, oxidation, deposits and wear that must be removed before penetrant inspection can see anything, and the cleaning and stripping steps become part of the inspection's validity. Technicians have to distinguish service damage from manufacturing discontinuities, and accept or reject against repair criteria rather than drawing tolerances. Repair work also brings the FAA into the picture: a shop repairing engine parts generally operates as a Part 145 repair station, with a repair station manual and training program the FAA oversees, while the engine maker's repair procedures specify the inspections. The written practice has to cover all of this, and the personnel files have to show technicians were trained and examined on repair inspection, not just new-part inspection.

We help these suppliers extend their written practice and procedures to the repair scope, prepare specific examination blueprints built from the repair procedures technicians actually use, and map the repair station manual against the written practice so the FAA and the engine maker's auditors find one consistent rule. The aviation NDT consulting page covers the maintenance side of this in more detail.

Fluorescent penetrant: the process every engine auditor tests

High-sensitivity fluorescent penetrant inspection is the workhorse of engine hardware, and an AC7114/1 audit of an engine supplier's line is thorough. The auditor will want to follow a part from pre-cleaning through any etch the specification requires, penetrant application and dwell, removal or emulsification, drying, developer and inspection, checking each step against the procedure and the customer specification. Booth conditions, UV-A and visible light measurements, known-defect panel results, materials qualification and contamination checks on in-use materials all appear in the log review, and the auditor compares them with ASTM E1417 and the engine maker's own requirements.

The documentation failures we see in Connecticut engine shops tend to be procedural rather than technical: a procedure that allows a process window the customer specification does not, a log that records a check but not the instrument used, a sensitivity level on the routing that differs from the one the line was set up for, or an evaluation done by someone certified in penetrant but not for the technique in use. We line up procedure, customer specification and log form, mark every mismatch and draft the corrections for approval. The aerospace penetrant compliance page lists the controls in detail.

Eddy current and ultrasonic on critical rotating parts

Disks, shafts and other critical rotating parts are inspected by eddy current at features such as bolt holes and slots and by ultrasonic methods at the forging and machining stages. These techniques are tightly defined by the engine maker, and auditors expect every parameter, reference standard and acceptance rule to be written into an approved technique. Your eddy current Level 3 approves eddy current techniques; Atlantis supports that work on the documentation side, checking traceability from part number to technique to reference standard to certified technician.

On the ultrasonic side, we review technique sheets, reference block certifications and scan plans, and check that examination specimens reflect the product forms and techniques technicians use. The aim is a file in which an auditor can pick any inspection record and walk backward to every control behind it without asking anyone to remember anything.

Engine maker requirements on top of NAS 410

Engine makers rarely stop at NAS 410. Their supplier quality requirements and NDT process specifications commonly add approval of the supplier's NDT procedures, notification before significant process changes, specific training or examination for particular part families, and rules on who may disposition indications. A Hartford-area supplier serving more than one engine program carries all of these at once, often in documents revised on different schedules.

We build a requirements matrix that lists each customer document and revision, what it adds to NAS 410, where your written practice or procedures meet it, and what evidence proves it. That matrix lets your Responsible Level 3 approve a written practice that stays general while customer-specific rules live in controlled appendices, and it gives the next auditor a quick map of the program. The structure of such a written practice is described on written practice development for aerospace.

Growing the workforce: Level 1 Limited and new hires

Capacity growth means new technicians, and NAS 410 gives engine shops a tool that is often underused: the Level 1 Limited category, for a person certified to perform one specific, narrowly defined operation, such as a single repetitive inspection on one product, under written instructions. Used well, it lets a shop bring people onto a high-volume line quickly while keeping their authority tightly bounded. Used carelessly, it produces certifications whose scope nobody can state, which is exactly what an auditor will ask about.

The documentation has to make the limit unmistakable. The certification record should name the operation, the part or part family, the work instruction and the acceptance authority, if any, and the written practice should define how Limited personnel are trained, examined and supervised. For new hires at Level 1 and Level 2, the training plan should tie each course to an approved outline and a qualified instructor, with hours recorded against the minimums. We draft the Level 1 Limited provisions, certification templates and training plans for your Responsible Level 3 to approve, and check existing Limited certifications for scope statements that would not survive an audit question.

Interrupted service and recertification in busy engine shops

When volume swings, technicians move between methods, shifts and product lines, and some stop working in a method for a stretch. NAS 410 requires the written practice to say what happens when a certified person has not performed in a method for longer than the standard allows, and auditors check whether anyone has drifted past that point without the required re-examination. Recertification is a related trap: certifications that lapsed quietly while the technician kept stamping reports are among the most serious findings an auditor can write.

We set up a register that tracks each technician's last documented work in each method, certification and recertification dates, and annual vision results, and we review the last year of records for anyone who crossed a limit. Your Level 3 decides what to do about each case. Ongoing tracking is easier in a system such as certificate tracking, and our expired certifications guide explains why spreadsheets tend to miss these dates.

The documents we prepare for approval

  1. A redlined written practice measured against NAS 410, with EN 4179 noted for European engine programs and each customer's additions referenced.
  2. A Responsible Level 3 designation file showing methods held and how other methods are covered.
  3. Personnel record packs: training against approved outlines, experience, general, specific and practical examinations, vision, certification and recertification.
  4. Outside agency agreements for any external training or examination provider, named in the written practice.
  5. Procedure and technique registers with approval and revision status, cross-referenced to customer specifications.
  6. Process control, calibration and reference standard registers for each NDT line.
  7. Corrective action packages after an audit: root cause, containment, correction and objective evidence for each finding.

See training records and certificates and AC7114 examination records for what each file should hold.

Revision 6 for Connecticut engine suppliers

The December 2025 edition of NAS 410, Revision 6, introduces Appendix D, through which experienced Level 2 personnel build up points for designated NDT activities until they qualify to attempt their first Level 3 examination; AIA also presents the edition as tightening up how certification requirements are worded. Engine suppliers should expect their customers to set their own expectations for adopting it. We prepare a side-by-side of your written practice against the new edition, flag what must change, and draft the revised text and a transition note for your Level 3. The NAS 410 explainer and NAS 410 versus SNT-TC-1A give the background.

Working with Atlantis in the Hartford area

Document review and drafting happen remotely, with any export-controlled material handled on your terms. A site visit covers the mock audit, in which your quality lead and our Level III tour each NDT line together, draw technician files unannounced and watch an inspection run from its approved technique sheet. To start, send your written practice, your certified personnel roster, the engine maker specifications and purchase order quality clauses you work to, and the last Nadcap or customer audit report. Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness explains the audit itself.

Atlantis also offers aerospace NDT training for East Hartford employers built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, third-party inspection in East Hartford and penetrant testing in Hartford. The training follows the ASNT document; in a NAS 410 program your Responsible Level 3 decides whether any outside hours can be credited. For the service as offered nationwide, see NAS 410 audit compliance documentation.

faq.q: We are moving from new-part manufacture into engine repair. What changes in our NDT documentation?
faq.a: The written practice and procedures must cover inspection of service-exposed parts, including cleaning and coating removal before penetrant, recognition of service damage and acceptance against repair criteria. Specific examinations should be built from the repair procedures your technicians use, and the repair station manual must agree with the written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis act as a Responsible Level 3 or certify technicians to NAS 410?
faq.a: No on all counts. Atlantis holds no Responsible Level 3 designation for any client, issues no NAS 410 certifications and runs no NAS 410 courses or exams. Our deliverables are drafts and reviews, which your designated Level 3 signs off and your company puts into effect.

faq.q: Who should approve our eddy current techniques for engine disks?
faq.a: A Level 3 certified in eddy current, usually your own, since eddy current is not among the five methods in which Atlantis holds Level III. We can organize and check the eddy current records for traceability, but the technical approval belongs to your eddy current Level 3.

faq.q: Our penetrant procedure allows a wider dwell window than one customer's specification. Is that a finding?
faq.a: It can be, if parts for that customer are processed outside the customer's window. Either tighten the procedure for that customer through a controlled appendix or technique sheet, or show that those parts always run within the narrower limits. The record must prove it, not just the intent.

faq.q: A technician has not done ultrasonic work for months. Can they go back to it?
faq.a: Only as your written practice allows for interrupted service. If the gap exceeds the limit it sets in line with NAS 410, re-examination is needed before the person works in the method again. We can review your records to find anyone in that position.

faq.q: Do Part 145 repair stations have to follow NAS 410?
faq.a: The FAA does not require NAS 410 by name. Repair stations follow their FAA-accepted repair station manual and the maintenance data they work to, and engine makers and customers often require NAS 410 or an equivalent written practice. In practice, most engine repair suppliers here run a NAS 410 program.

faq.q: How do we handle engine maker requirements that change on different schedules?
faq.a: Keep a requirements matrix that records each customer document, its current revision, what it adds and where your program meets it, reviewed by your Level 3 when any revision changes. Customer-specific rules then live in controlled appendices instead of being scattered through procedures.

faq.q: Do you come to Connecticut for the mock audit?
faq.a: Yes. Watching inspections and sampling files unannounced only works in person, so that step happens at your plant. Drafting and document review stay remote, and the visiting team travels from the Houston or Hyderabad office.

faq.q: Can our technicians use Atlantis training toward NAS 410 certification?
faq.a: The Atlantis curriculum is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, so it is not a NAS 410 course. Inside a NAS 410 program, crediting hours from any external course is a call for your Responsible Level 3, documented as the written practice requires. See NDT training in East Hartford for course content.
